name: Wendy Yilmaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work on the repairs team for a housing association, which is a non-profit landlord with about four thousand flats across the east side. I'm paired with Gloria, who's been doing this for thirty years. We get a list each morning on a tablet: a tripping fuse box here, a dead smoke alarm there, a tenant who swears her oven is giving her shocks. Most days it's eight or nine jobs, lots of stairs, and a lot of talking to tenants.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that it matters. If an old man's heating cuts out in January, we're the ones who get it back on. What wears me out is the backlog, because there's always more broken stuff than people to fix it, and tenants are angry by the time we arrive. And I'm still slow at fault-finding; Gloria finds the problem in five minutes when it takes me forty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: So the tablet stays a tablet. Fine by me, I quite like my job as it is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say on the group chat with the other juniors that it's good news, honestly. Our work is fixing real things in real homes. I'd say if the hype is over, maybe the money goes back into staff instead of software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'm in a decent spot. The housing association isn't going anywhere, the repairs never stop, and my union got us a pay deal last year. Broken fuse boxes in four thousand flats are the most secure job I could ask for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep at it and ask Gloria to let me lead the fault-finding on more jobs, even if it's slower. I'd keep putting money aside for a deposit with Sanna; we've got about three months of bills saved. And I'd sign up for the fire alarm course the association pays for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty calm. Bit bored by the idea, maybe, but calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use AI now and then. What for, right now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly to write up the job notes when a repair is messy, so the next person knows what I found. Sometimes I ask it to explain a fault in plain words before I ring Gloria. It's handy, but I check everything, because once it told me a colour code that was just wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned a deposit. How far off is that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Years, if I'm honest. Sanna drives buses and I'm on a junior wage, and flat prices are silly. We'd probably need a shared-ownership place, where you buy part and rent the rest.

say: I'd say it's **good news** for people who fix real things.
I'd say money should go into **staff, not software**.
think: I think the **housing association** job is about as secure as work gets.
I think last year's **union pay deal** shows the job is protected.
do: Ask Gloria to let me **lead fault-finding** on more jobs.
Keep saving for a **deposit with Sanna**.
Sign up for the association's **fire alarm course**.
feel: I feel **calm**, and a little bored by the idea.
S0.quote: Broken fuse boxes in four thousand flats are the most secure job I could ask for.
fieldNote: Wendy's **non-profit employer** and endless repairs give her real security.
Her main weakness is **slow fault-finding**, and she knows it.
She already **checks AI answers** after one wrong colour code.

steps.text: Lead the fault-finding on more repair jobs with Gloria watching
Keep saving towards a shared-ownership flat with Sanna
Take the association's paid fire alarm course

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can already see where that lands at work. Our call centre, the repairs desk, is twenty people booking jobs and taking complaints.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say publicly that the association should keep the repairs desk staff and move them into other roles, not cut them. I'd raise it at our union meeting, because those are our colleagues. I'd say AI should help the backlog, not shrink the payroll.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my job barely changes, but the people around me get hammered. If a chatbot books every repair, the twenty people on our repairs desk are the first ones gone, and I know every one of them. For me, maybe I get better job notes and a smarter list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start using the AI more for fault guides, carefully, because once Gloria's colleagues are using it I'd want to keep up. I'd go to the union meetings on the repairs desk. I'd keep saving, same as now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. My stomach drops a bit thinking about Bea on the desk, who's a single mum.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Bea if the cuts were announced?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her to come to the union meeting with me and not sign anything that night. And I'd ask the manager whether there are trainee spots on our team, because Bea knows every block better than I do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Bea on your team be a threat to your own place?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, a bit, I won't lie. But there's always more broken stuff than people. I'd rather have her on the vans than lose her to some warehouse.

say: I'd say the association should **retrain the repairs desk**, not cut it.
I'd say AI should **clear the backlog**, not shrink the payroll.
think: I think **my job** barely changes, but colleagues get hit.
I fear the twenty people on the **repairs desk** go first.
do: Use AI more for **fault guides**, checking everything.
Attend **union meetings** about the repairs desk.
feel: I feel **uneasy**, mostly about Bea, a single mum on the desk.
S1.quote: If a chatbot books every repair, the twenty people on our repairs desk are the first ones gone, and I know every one of them.
fieldNote: Wendy instantly maps the change to the **repairs desk** next to her.
She'd push for **trainee spots** even though it adds competition for her.
Her own **hands-on work** stays safe here.

steps.text: Use an AI fault guide on tricky repairs, checking it with Gloria
Bring Bea to the union meeting about the repairs desk
Keep saving a fixed amount each month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years for the thinking part and robots in five. That's when I'd be 32, finally quick at the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's reckless to drop this on people with no plan. I'd want laws that stop landlords like ours replacing staff without a deal. And I'd say it on the union page.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the first two years I'm fine, maybe even busier, because the planning and booking get faster and they send us to more jobs. Climbing six flights of stairs to a smoke alarm keeps my job safe until 2031, and after that I honestly don't know. A robot that climbs stairs and talks to an angry tenant, though, maybe not right away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the two years to get my full licence and the fire alarm and emergency lighting tickets, because they're things a person signs off. I'd stop the deposit plan and keep the cash liquid, so around five months of bills. I'd push the union for a no-redundancy deal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not panicked, because I'd have time to move, but it's my whole plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Sanna cut first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The holiday to see her family in the summer, probably. And the gym. We'd keep paying into savings, because that's the thing that buys time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Earlier you said you only trust AI once it's proven. Would that change here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In this one it's proven by definition, isn't it? So yes, I'd use it every day to learn faster. I'd still double-check the colour codes.

say: I'd call it **reckless** to arrive with no plan.
I'd want laws stopping landlords **replacing staff** without a deal.
think: I think the first **two years** may make me busier, not idle.
I don't know what happens once **robots** climb stairs in 2031.
do: Get my **full licence** plus fire and emergency lighting tickets.
Pause the **deposit plan** and keep five months of bills in cash.
Push the union for a **no-redundancy deal**.
feel: I feel **anxious**, because it hits my whole plan.
S2.quote: Climbing six flights of stairs to a smoke alarm keeps my job safe until 2031, and after that I honestly don't know.
fieldNote: Wendy grasps the **three-year gap** between thinking AI and robots and plans around it.
She moves her savings from **deposit to buffer** without hesitation.
Her **steady streak** flips once a tool is proven.

steps.text: Get the full licence and fire and emergency lighting tickets
Pause the flat deposit and keep five months of bills in cash
Push the union for a no-redundancy deal at the association
Use AI daily to learn fault-finding faster

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years, then robots by 2034. Okay. That feels more like something you can steer through.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment for governments and the association to plan together, not wait. I'd be the annoying one at union meetings asking what the plan is. Online, probably the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd be a properly qualified electrician with a few years in by the time the robots come, which matters a lot. By 2034 I want to be the person who checks the robot's work, not the person it replaced.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the licence, then the inspection and testing qualification, because that's the job of checking work. I'd keep saving for the deposit but slower, maybe half. And I'd start using the AI regularly so I'm not the one who's scared of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious but steady. I'd have a plan, at least.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who's the person you'd worry about most on your team?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gloria, funnily enough. She's 58, brilliant, and she hates the tablet. If robots come at 62 for her, she won't retrain, she'll just go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would that change anything you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try to learn everything Gloria knows in the next five years, the stuff that isn't written down. Like which blocks have aluminium wiring and which tenants have dogs.

say: I'd say governments and the association must **plan together** now.
I'd keep asking at union meetings for **the plan**.
think: I think I'll be **properly qualified** by the time robots come.
I want to **check the robot's work**, not be replaced by it.
do: Take the licence, then the **inspection and testing** qualification.
Save for the **deposit at half pace**.
Use **AI regularly** so it doesn't scare me.
feel: I feel **anxious but steady**, because I'd have a plan.
S3.quote: By 2034 I want to be the person who checks the robot's work, not the person it replaced.
fieldNote: Wendy chooses **inspection and testing** as the role that outlasts robots.
She worries more for **Gloria**, 58, than for herself.
She'd harvest Gloria's **unwritten knowledge** while there's time.

steps.text: Take the inspection and testing qualification after the licence
Save for the deposit at half the usual pace
Use AI tools weekly for job notes and fault guides
Write down Gloria's knowledge of each block before she retires

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, robots by 2039. I'd be nearly 40. That's long enough to have a whole different career by then, if I wanted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty if it's used well, and that it's on employers and government to use it. I'd say it to anyone who'd listen at the union.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'd be fine. Ten years is long enough for me to become the senior electrician that the new kids follow up the stairs. And maybe by then I run a team, or train apprentices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on the normal way: licence, then inspection, then maybe the supervisor course in five years. We'd go ahead with the shared-ownership flat. I'd keep using AI now and then, as it gets better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm, with a little uneasy feeling at the back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why go ahead with the flat in this one but not the fast one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because with ten years I'd have most of a mortgage term's start paid down with a qualified wage. In the fast one, I don't want a mortgage on a junior wage when I don't know what my job is in 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the uneasy bit at the back?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That everyone says ten years and then does nothing for nine. I've seen how slow the association is to fix a lift. I'd want to make sure we actually start.

say: I'd say ten years is **plenty if used well**.
I'd say it's on **employers and government** to use it.
think: I think I'd **be fine** with a decade to prepare.
I could become the **senior electrician** others follow.
do: Keep to the plan: licence, inspection, then a **supervisor course**.
Use AI **now and then** as it improves.
feel: I feel **mostly calm**, with a little unease at the back.
S4.quote: Ten years is long enough for me to become the senior electrician that the new kids follow up the stairs.
fieldNote: Wendy's **flat decision** tracks the warning time very precisely.
Her unease is about **institutions wasting** the decade.
She pictures herself as a **future trainer** of apprentices.

steps.text: Take the supervisor course after five licensed years
Buy the shared-ownership flat with Sanna
Keep the licence, then inspection plan on track

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd still be learning when everything moved. What would help is a law that public landlords can't cut staff without retraining them, and a paid course for juniors like me to get qualified fast.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about tenants. A robot might fix the fuse box, but the woman on the ninth floor mostly wants someone to tell her she's not going to burn down.

headlineQuote: A robot might fix the fuse box, but the woman on the ninth floor mostly wants someone to tell her she's not going to burn down.
portrait: Wendy is a **27-year-old junior** on a housing association repairs team.
She's steady with tech: she uses **AI for job notes** but checks everything.
She worries about **colleagues** first, like Bea on the repairs desk and Gloria, 58.
She plans around **qualifications**, aiming to check robots' work, and times her flat purchase to the warning.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because she'd still be learning when everything moved.
whatWouldHelp: A law that **public landlords retrain** staff before cutting them.
